speakingQ3.c: Concept: habituation, where repeated non-threatening exposure reduces an instinctive fear response; the professor's example is prairie dogs learning that frequently passing humans are not dangerous.

speakingQ3.g: Population size is shaped by predator numbers, which reduce prey, and by climate, which can lengthen the breeding season and add extra reproductive cycles.
speakingQ3.k: 개체군 크기는 포식자 수와 기후에 따른 번식 기간 같은 요인에 의해 달라진다는 개념을 예시로 설명함
speakingQ3.c: Concept: population size depends on regulating factors such as predation and weather. Professor's example: more owls cut the mouse population, and an early warm spring gives rabbits an extra breeding cycle, raising their numbers.

speakingQ3.g: Verbal agreements without written terms can lead to disputes when the two parties assume different scopes of work.
speakingQ3.k: 구두 계약은 작업 범위를 명확히 적지 않으면 서로 다른 기대에서 분쟁이 생기기 쉽다는 개념을 친구 사례로 보여줌
speakingQ3.c: Concept: informal verbal agreements leave scope ambiguous; Example: a contractor friend builds a fence under a spoken deal, then the client insists on painting too, and he gives in reluctantly.

speakingQ3.g: A memorization method that links items in order to familiar landmarks along a route, then mentally walks the route to retrieve them.
speakingQ3.k: 익숙한 장소의 경로 위 랜드마크에 기억할 항목을 순서대로 연결해 떠올리는 기억법 설명
speakingQ3.c: Concept: the method of loci, pairing sequential items with mental landmarks on a familiar path; professor's example: memorizing planets' order from the Sun by assigning each planet to a landmark on a walk from the dorm to the student center.

speakingQ3.g: Skunks use a conspicuous color pattern paired with a foul spray, so predators learn to associate the look with the unpleasant experience and avoid them afterward.
speakingQ3.k: 스컹크는 눈에 띄는 무늬로 포식자에게 자신을 알리고, 분사 방어로 한 번 겪은 포식자가 그 무늬를 기억해 다시 피하게 만든다.
speakingQ3.c: Concept: a conspicuous appearance combined with a noxious defense teaches predators to avoid the animal; Example: a wolf sprayed by a skunk learns to stay away from its black-and-white markings.

speakingQ3.g: When people feel their freedom is being restricted, they tend to want the restricted thing more and may act to reclaim it, even when it has no real value to them.
speakingQ3.k: 사람들은 자유가 제한되면 그 자유를 더 강하게 원하게 되어, 금지된 행동을 오히려 더 많이 하려 한다.
speakingQ3.c: Concept: psychological reactance, the urge to restore threatened freedom. Professor's examples: a child sneaking into a banned playground, and townspeople stockpiling soap before a harmless ingredient is banned.

speakingQ3.g: A crow picks the largest shellfish and drops it from a precise height so the shell breaks with minimal wasted effort.
speakingQ3.k: 까마귀가 큰 조개를 골라 약 5미터 높이에서 떨어뜨려 껍질을 깨고, 불필요한 에너지 낭비를 피하는 채집 방식
speakingQ3.c: concept: optimal energy-efficient foraging; example: a crow choosing large shellfish and dropping them from about five meters to crack the shell

speakingQ3.g: A skill learned through repeated practice can be recalled automatically after years of disuse, even when the person cannot explain the steps consciously; the professor illustrates this with returning to guitar playing.
speakingQ3.k: 오랫동안 연습하지 않은 기술도 몸이 기억해 다시 쉽게 수행할 수 있다는 개념을 교수가 기타 연주 경험으로 설명함
speakingQ3.c: Concept: procedural memory lets learned motor skills persist without conscious recall. Example: the professor picked up a guitar after years and could still play his favorite songs, though he could not describe the finger movements.

speakingQ3.g: Memory recall tends to be stronger when it happens in the same setting where the information was learned, as shown by a student's experience of forgetting facts in an unfamiliar place and recovering them in the original classroom.
speakingQ3.k: 학습 장소와 떠올리는 장소가 같을 때 기억이 더 잘 회상된다는 개념을 학생 시절 경험으로 설명함
speakingQ3.c: the concept of context-dependent memory and the professor's example of a student group who struggled to recall plant facts at home but performed well back in the classroom

speakingQ3.g: A cookie company uses a bear mascot across packaging, ads, and product shape to make children like its product and associate the character with cookies, boosting sales.
speakingQ3.k: 빅베어 쿠키는 곰 캐릭터를 광고와 제품에 활용해 아이들의 호감과 기억을 끌어내 경쟁사보다 많이 팔았다.
speakingQ3.c: Concept: using a recurring animal mascot to build brand recognition; Professor's example: Big Bear Cookies, whose bear character appears on boxes, TV ads, and the cookie shape itself, making children remember and buy its cookies.

speakingQ3.g: People often adjust their appearance and behavior to signal responsibility and respect to others, sometimes without realizing it.
speakingQ3.k: 사람들은 타인에게 좋은 인상을 주기 위해 겉모습과 행동을 의식적으로 또는 무의식적으로 바꾼다.
speakingQ3.c: Concept: impression management, where people tailor their looks and actions to shape how others judge them; Professor's examples: dressing up for a class presentation, and cleaning the car and switching to classical music before driving the university president.

speakingQ3.g: A parent taught a toddler handwashing by splitting it into small steps and adding each new step only after the previous ones were mastered.
speakingQ3.k: 아이에게 손 씻기를 한 번에 가르치지 않고 단계별로 나눠 하나씩 익히게 한 경험
speakingQ3.c: Concept: breaking a complex task into simpler steps and teaching them sequentially (backward/forward chaining); Professor's example: teaching her three-year-old daughter to wash hands by adding one step at a time

speakingQ3.g: Looking past a problem's obvious surface explanation to its underlying cause can lead to an effective fix, illustrated by a company whose absenteeism fell after it addressed employees' health-related causes.
speakingQ3.k: 겉으로 드러난 원인보다 숨은 근본 원인을 찾아 해결하면 문제가 개선된다는 개념을 회사 결근 사례로 설명함
speakingQ3.c: Concept: uncovering indirect root causes of a problem; Professor's example: a company's absenteeism traced to poor diet and inactivity, which it addressed by adding a gym and healthier cafeteria options, after which attendance improved.

speakingQ3.g: When one fish species that eats algae disappears, other species feeding on the same algae expand to fill its role, keeping the reef stable.
speakingQ3.k: 산호초에서 한 종이 사라져도 같은 먹이를 먹는 다른 종들이 균형을 유지해 생태계가 안정된다는 내용
speakingQ3.c: concept: ecological redundancy (several species share one food source so losing one is compensated); professor's example: a coral reef where pollution wiped out an algae-eating fish but other algae-eaters multiplied and the reef recovered its prior appearance

speakingQ3.g: Leafcutter ants split food transport into three coordinated roles, each handling one stage, which speeds up the work and reduces individual fatigue.
speakingQ3.k: 잎꾼개미는 세 무리로 나뉘어 나무 위 채취, 잎 절단, 둥지 운반을 분업해 먹이를 더 빠르고 효율적으로 옮긴다.
speakingQ3.c: concept-example: the professor illustrates division of labor with leafcutter ants, showing how three stages of collecting, cutting, and carrying leaves work together.

speakingQ3.g: A desert shrub deters neighboring roots with a chemical signal, securing water and space for its own roots.
speakingQ3.k: 사막 식물 creosote는 화학물질을 분비해 주변 식물의 뿌리가 자기 쪽으로 자라지 못하게 하여 물과 공간을 확보한다.
speakingQ3.c: concept: allelopathic chemical signaling that repels competing roots; example: the creosote plant in the desert

speakingQ3.g: Two ant species of different sizes share a hollow branch: the small ones feed on the big ones' leftover scraps and, by eating them, keep the nest clean, which benefits both.
speakingQ3.k: 작은 개미와 큰 개미가 같은 나무 가지 안에 살며, 작은 개미는 큰 개미가 남긴 음식 부스러기를 먹고 집을 청결하게 유지해 큰 개미도 이득을 얻는다.

speakingQ3.g: A thirteen-year-old, pressured by friends watching, complies with a parent's chore request but deliberately displays reluctance to signal to peers that they are no longer a child.
speakingQ3.k: 열세 살 아이가 친구 앞에서 부모의 지시를 따르면서도 일부러 불만을 드러내는 행동을 통해 또래에게 자신이 어린아이가 아님을 보여주려 한다는 예시

speakingQ3.g: Grey squirrels fake some burial holes with twigs or stones to mislead nearby birds like blue jays, which then waste effort digging and give up.
speakingQ3.k: 다람쥐가 새에게 먹이를 빼앗기지 않으려고 일부 구멍에만 도토리를 넣고 나머지는 속여 가짜로 묻는다.
speakingQ3.c: Concept: squirrels deceive predators by faking caches; Professor's example: grey squirrels dig many holes but fill only a few with nuts, leading blue jays to find little food.

speakingQ3.g: A researcher testing an office exercise program couldn't measure its true effect because the control group overheard the treatment group and started doing the exercises too.
speakingQ3.k: 한 연구자가 사무실 직원들의 피로 예방 운동 효과를 실험했으나, 대조군이 실험군의 운동을 듣고 따라 하면서 효과를 정확히 측정할 수 없게 되었다.
speakingQ3.c: concept: control group contamination from information leakage between groups; example: office workers' stretching study where Group B copied Group A and the effect became unmeasurable

speakingQ3.g: The professor shares a personal dinner-party story to illustrate how people overestimate how easily others can detect their hidden feelings.
speakingQ3.k: 교수는 자신이 싫어하는 재료가 들어간 저녁 식사 경험을 예로 들어, 사람들이 자신의 감정을 실제보다 훨씬 쉽게 알아챌 거라고 과대평가하는 현상을 설명한다.
speakingQ3.c: Concept: people overestimate how noticeable their private feelings are to others. Professor's example: he worried a friend could tell he disliked a disliked-ingredient dish, but the friend and another guest had noticed nothing.

speakingQ3.g: A caterpillar senses an approaching wasp through air vibrations picked up by fine body hairs and drops to safety.
speakingQ3.k: 애벌레가 공기 중 진동을 감지하는 털로 천적의 접근을 알아채고 떨어져 몸을 피한다
speakingQ3.c: concept: sensory hairs detect air vibrations from a wasp's wings; example: caterpillar drops from branch to escape predation

speakingQ3.g: Having too many options can make a simple purchase exhausting and leave the buyer anxious rather than satisfied, as the professor illustrates with a jeans-shopping experience.
speakingQ3.k: 선택지가 많아지면 오히려 결정이 어려워지고 만족도가 떨어진다는 현상을 교수가 청바지 쇼핑 경험으로 설명한다.
speakingQ3.c: Concept: choice overload, where many options make decisions harder; Example: the professor's jeans shopping trip, which took far longer and left him anxious.

speakingQ3.g: Rigid rules meant to protect learning, such as barring late students, can end up reducing the education they were designed to secure.
speakingQ3.k: 지나치게 엄격한 지각 규정은 학생의 학습 기회를 오히려 빼앗을 수 있다.
speakingQ3.c: Concept: rules meant to support education can backfire. Professor's example: a school that refuses entry to any student arriving late, so the student misses the whole class and the learning it offers.

speakingQ3.g: The professor describes how making a morning running date with a friend helped him stick to a training routine he otherwise would have skipped.
speakingQ3.k: 교수가 자신의 달리기 훈련 사례를 들어, 친구와 약속을 정해 스스로를 구속하는 방식이 실천을 돕는다는 점을 보여준다.
speakingQ3.c: concept: self-commitment through an external promise (commitment device); example: professor's 10K training, where a friend-arranged morning run overcame his urge to sleep in

speakingQ4.g: Researchers infer that very young infants grasp basic addition by measuring how long they stare when an expected outcome doesn't occur.
speakingQ4.k: 생후 5개월 아기도 기본적인 덧셈 개념을 이해하는지를 인형 실험으로 확인한 연구
speakingQ4.c: Concept: infants as young as five months may understand that one plus one makes two; professor's example: a doll-hiding experiment where babies stare longer when only one doll appears after two were placed behind a screen, showing surprise at the mismatch.

speakingQ4.s: broad vs. narrow definitions of money
speakingQ4.g: Money can be defined broadly as anything usable for purchases, including barter goods, while a narrower definition covers only what sellers are legally required to accept.
speakingQ4.k: 돈은 구매에 쓰일 수 있는 모든 것으로 넓게 정의할 수 있고, 법정 화폐는 판매자가 반드시 받아야 하는 좁은 의미의 돈이다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: money is broadly anything used to buy goods or services, and narrowly the legal tender that must be accepted; Example: a taxi driver paying a farmer with cash versus bartering vegetables for a ride, where only the cash is legally required.

speakingQ4.g: Advertisers use subtle persuasion, such as repetition and celebrity endorsement, to make consumers believe claims even when they are untrue.
speakingQ4.k: 광고는 반복 노출과 유명인 추천을 통해 사실이 아니어도 소비자가 믿게 만드는 설득 전략을 사용한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: repeated exposure and endorsement by admired celebrities make people accept claims. Example: a car ad that repeats a roominess slogan despite a small car, and a race driver praising a low-performance car's speed.

speakingQ4.g: Artists combine visual elements like color and texture to convey emotion, and the way they paint, such as bold or delicate strokes, shapes how viewers feel.
speakingQ4.k: 미술 작품은 색채, 질감, 선 등 시각 요소를 결합해 감정과 메시지를 전달하며, 붓질과 색 선택이 관람자의 정서를 바꾼다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: visual elements such as color and texture combine to express mood and meaning. Example: a painting with bold reds, oranges, and broad rough strokes evokes a wilder, more chaotic feeling than one with tiny smooth strokes and pale colors.

speakingQ4.g: Motivation splits into extrinsic drives tied to outside rewards and intrinsic drives rooted in personal enjoyment, with the intrinsic kind usually lasting longer.
speakingQ4.k: 동기는 외적 보상에 따른 외재적 동기와 내면의 즐거움에서 나오는 내재적 동기로 나뉘며, 내재적 동기가 더 오래 지속된다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: extrinsic motivation (outside rewards, e.g., a child paid for chores) versus intrinsic motivation (inner enjoyment); professor's example: exercising at the gym for personal satisfaction over five years.

speakingQ4.g: The professor distinguishes effortful attention from effortless attention and suggests using a surprising demonstration to capture the effortless kind, which lasts longer.
speakingQ4.k: 교수는 학생 주의집중의 두 유형(의지적 주의와 비의지적 주의)을 설명하고, 흥미로운 시연으로 후자를 활용하라고 제안한다.
speakingQ4.c: concept-example: voluntary (active) vs. involuntary (passive) attention, illustrated by bringing a live frog into a biology lesson

speakingQ4.s: product quality factors and consumer choice
speakingQ4.g: Consumers judge quality by reliability and features; since reliability is now similar across brands, features drive the choice and manufacturers add more of them.
speakingQ4.k: 제품 품질은 신뢰성과 기능으로 나뉘며, 신뢰성이 대체로 비슷해진 오늘날에는 소비자가 부가 기능을 보고 제품을 고른다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: product quality has two factors, reliability (working as expected without unexpected defects) and features (extras that add ease of use or appeal). Professor's example: modern cars, where reliability is high everywhere, so buyers compare electric windows, sunroofs, air-conditioning, and stereos.

speakingQ4.g: Companies can set a new product's launch price high to signal quality and skim early profits, or set it low to undercut rivals and win market share, then recoup profits through related accessories.
speakingQ4.k: 기업이 신제품을 처음 출시할 때 쓰는 두 가지 가격 전략, 즉 높게 시작해 점차 내리는 방식과 낮게 시작해 시장을 점유하는 방식을 설명한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: high-initial-price (skimming) versus low-initial-price (penetration) strategies; professor's example: early high-tech gadgets priced premium, and a new computer maker pricing low and profiting from accessories.

speakingQ4.g: Plants defend themselves from insects in two ways: physical traits that block insects from landing or feeding, and chemicals released during an attack that make insects stop eating.
speakingQ4.k: 식물은 물리적 특징과 화학물질을 이용해 곤충의 공격으로부터 스스로를 보호한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: plants have physical and chemical defenses against insects. Professor's examples: passion plant leaves covered in dense spiky hairs that stop insects from landing; potato plant releasing a chemical when attacked that makes the feeding insect feel full and stop eating.

speakingQ4.g: A lecture describes an experiment suggesting that infants who cry at other babies' crying may be feeling empathy rather than merely reacting to the noise.
speakingQ4.k: 아기들이 다른 아기의 울음에 반응하는 것이 단순한 소음 때문이 아니라 공감 때문일 수 있다는 실험 이야기
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: infant empathy (concern for others beyond direct self-reaction); professor's example: babies crying more at another's recording than at their own, implying empathy rather than noise sensitivity

speakingQ4.g: Good interior design balances unity, created by repeating similar elements like colors, with contrast that breaks the sameness, and too much of either creates problems.
speakingQ4.k: 인테리어 디자인에서는 통일성과 대비를 균형 있게 써야 하며, 색을 활용한 예시로 설명한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: unity and contrast must be balanced; Professor's example: matching green walls, sofa, and rug show unity, while bright red cushions on the green sofa add contrast, but excess contrast makes a room chaotic.

speakingQ4.g: Demand for a good can also shift with the prices of related goods: substitutes rise in demand when another's price climbs, while complements fall together.
speakingQ4.k: 상품 수요는 가격뿐 아니라 관련 상품의 가격에도 영향을 받으며, 대체재와 보완재가 이를 보여준다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept and example: the professor defines substitute goods using butter and margarine, and complementary goods using compact discs and CD players.

speakingQ4.g: Sea animals evolve camouflage to blend into their surroundings and evade predators, either through fixed colors and shapes or through rapid color change.
speakingQ4.k: 바다 동물들은 포식자를 피하려고 주변 환경에 섞이는 위장술을 발달시켰으며, 고정된 모양·색과 빠르게 변하는 색이 그 예이다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: sea animal camouflage; professor's examples: Leafy Sea Dragon (permanent shape and color matching green plants, which fails in other habitats) vs. Cuttlefish (rapid color-shifting pigments that match any background).

speakingQ4.g: Deep-sea creatures evolved specialized traits, such as expandable jaws and light-producing organs, to catch food in an environment where it is scarce.
speakingQ4.k: 심해에서는 먹이가 부족해서 생물들이 큰 먹이를 삼키거나 빛을 내어 먹이를 잡는 적응 능력을 발달시켰다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: deep-sea organisms adapt to scarce food; example: the eel's expandable mouth and stomach for swallowing large prey, and the angler fish's light lure that attracts prey close enough to capture.

speakingQ4.g: The placement of a bird's eyes on its skull affects survival: forward-facing eyes aid precise hunting, while side-set eyes provide wide views for spotting predators.
speakingQ4.k: 새의 눈 위치(정면 vs 측면)는 먹이 찾기와 포식자 회피 등 생존에 각각 다른 방식으로 기여한다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: eye position in birds (forward-facing vs side-set eyes); professor's example: hawks hunting mice with forward eyes and ducks spotting foxes with side eyes

speakingQ4.g: Locus of control describes whether people see their life outcomes as governed internally or externally, and the lecturer illustrates how this shapes job-interview preparation and how each type interprets success or failure.
speakingQ4.k: 통제 소재 개념: 사람들이 삶의 통제력을 자신 안에서 찾는지 외부에서 찾는지에 따라 행동과 결과 해석이 달라진다는 설명
speakingQ4.c: Concept: locus of control (internal vs. external); professor's example: two job candidates, one internal who prepares hard and reflects on failure, one external who takes risks and attributes results to luck or interviewers' mood

speakingQ4.g: Cultural diffusion is the spread of customs, foods, or inventions between groups, often selectively, as with acupuncture being adopted without its underlying philosophy.
speakingQ4.k: 문화 확산은 한 집단의 문화 요소가 다른 집단으로 퍼지는 과정이며, 받아들여지는 것은 선택적이다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: cultural diffusion, the spreading of cultural items between groups over distance and time; Example: newspapers rely on borrowed writing, printing, and paper, and acupuncture is accepted in the US while its philosophy is not.

speakingQ4.g: Companies use target customers' age and location to decide when and where to advertise, illustrated with toy cars for children and boats for lakeside or coastal residents.
speakingQ4.k: 기업은 목표 고객의 연령과 거주 지역을 파악해 광고 시기와 장소를 정하며, 장난감 자동차와 보트 사례로 이를 설명한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: target customers' age and geographic location shape marketing strategy; Example: a toy car maker advertises during children's TV shows, and a boat maker advertises in areas near water.

speakingQ4.g: Sea birds evolved traits such as long, still wings that let them glide cheaply over vast ocean areas, and a keen sense of smell that helps them locate scattered prey from afar.
speakingQ4.k: 바다새들은 넓게 흩어진 먹이를 찾기 위해 긴 날개로 적은 에너지로 활공하고, 발달한 후각으로 멀리서 플랑크톤을 찾는 적응을 보인다.

speakingQ4.g: People unconsciously use defense mechanisms to shield themselves from painful feelings, illustrated by a woman who lost her dog and copes through fantasy and sublimation.
speakingQ4.k: 사람들은 괴로운 감정을 피하려고 무의식적으로 방어기제를 쓰며, 예로 잃어버린 개를 둔 여성의 공상과 승화가 제시된다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: defense mechanisms as unconscious self-protection from helplessness or emotional pain. Professor's example: a woman whose dog ran away uses fantasy (imagining the dog happy elsewhere) and sublimation (turning her loss into a dog-training school).

speakingQ4.g: Steam-powered machines moved cloth production from homes into factories, and workers gathering around those factories turned villages into cities.
speakingQ4.k: 산업혁명기에 증기 기계 도입으로 생산이 가정에서 공장으로 옮겨가고, 그 결과 공장 주변에 도시가 형성되었다.
speakingQ4.c: Two main changes of the Industrial Revolution: production moved from homes to factories, and factory towns grew into cities; the professor illustrates both with cloth weaving and a village factory.

speakingQ4.g: Animals living underground evolved physical traits to move efficiently through dense soil and to shield sensitive body parts, such as the eyes, from particles.
speakingQ4.k: 땅속에 사는 동물들이 흙을 헤치며 이동하고 눈 같은 민감한 부위를 보호하기 위해 진화한 신체 특징
speakingQ4.c: concept-example: the professor explains underground adaptations and uses the mole's wide claw-like front feet and hairy eye membranes as examples

speakingQ4.g: Carnivorous plants obtain nutrients by trapping insects because their soil is poor, and they use either active traps that move or passive traps that rely on sticky surfaces.
speakingQ4.k: 식충식물은 토양이 척박해 영양분을 곤충에서 얻으며, 능동형과 수동형 포획 방식으로 나뉜다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: carnivorous plants use active traps (movement) or passive traps (no moving parts); example: the Venus flytrap closes its hinged leaves to catch prey, while the sundew uses sticky hairs to glue insects in place.

speakingQ4.s: narrative point of view in fiction
speakingQ4.g: Writers choose a narrator type, and the choice shapes how much readers learn about characters and how they interpret events.
speakingQ4.k: 소설가는 서술자의 유형에 따라 독자가 인물을 이해하는 방식이 달라진다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: objective narrator reports only actions and speech, forcing readers to infer meaning; professor's example: omniscient narrator reveals a man's thoughts, such as nervousness and worry about his wife's opinion of his friend.

speakingQ4.g: Weathering breaks rocks apart through environmental exposure, mainly by water freezing in cracks and by plant roots widening them over time.
speakingQ4.k: 암석이 물의 동결과 식물 뿌리의 성장으로 갈라지고 부서지는 풍화 작용을 설명한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: weathering, the gradual breakdown of rocks through environmental exposure; Example: water freezing and expanding in cracks, and tree roots growing into rock fissures.

speakingQ4.g: Consumers judge a product partly by its container, so designs that are convenient to use or visually pleasing make products more appealing.
speakingQ4.k: 소비자는 제품 용기의 편리성과 외관도 함께 보고 구매를 결정하며, 이것이 브랜드 선택에 큰 영향을 준다.
speakingQ4.c: concept-example: the professor defines container design goals (convenience and appearance) and illustrates them with plastic condiment bottles and decorative cookie tins.

speakingQ4.g: Roman engineering advances, such as waterproof concrete bridges and long-distance aqueducts, let cities grow beyond river banks and past natural barriers.
speakingQ4.k: 로마의 기술 발전(수중 경화 콘크리트 다리와 수로교)이 도시가 강을 넘고 먼 곳까지 커질 수 있게 했다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: Roman technological advances allowed cities to expand beyond the limits that constrained earlier ancient cities. Example: hydraulic concrete bridges spanning wide rivers and aqueducts carrying water from distant mountains.

speakingQ4.g: Lakes are not permanent: they can vanish naturally when organic debris gradually fills them, or faster through human water extraction that outpaces refilling.
speakingQ4.k: 호수는 영구적이지 않으며, 자연적으로는 유기 퇴적물이 쌓여, 인위적으로는 물 펌핑으로 사라질 수 있다.

speakingQ4.g: When a single product's sales plateau, firms can broaden their offerings by reusing existing technology or by selling complementary goods to current customers.
speakingQ4.k: 시장 성장이 둔화되면 기업은 기존 자원을 활용해 제품을 다각화하여 새로운 고객과 매출을 확보할 수 있다.

speakingQ4.g: Some animals travel underground, which helps them avoid extreme heat and surprise prey by approaching unseen.
speakingQ4.k: 일부 동물은 땅속으로 이동하며, 이는 극한 온도를 피하고 먹이를 사냥하는 데 도움이 된다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: subsurface locomotion (underground movement); professor's example: a Sahara desert lizard that escapes heat and ambushes insects by sensing their vibrations.

speakingQ4.g: Arctic animals survive extreme cold mainly through body features that limit heat loss, such as insulated feet and compact bodies with short protruding parts.
speakingQ4.k: 북극 동물들은 추위에 견디기 위해 발의 보온 덮개와 작고 몸에서 덜 튀어나온 신체 구조를 발달시켰다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: body features that reduce heat loss in cold climates; professor's example: the Arctic snowy owl's feathered feet and the Arctic wolf's compact body with smaller ears and shorter legs.

speakingQ4.s: road impacts on wildlife and plants
speakingQ4.g: Roads spread invasive plant species that compete with native plants and split animal habitats into fragments, leaving animals short of food.
speakingQ4.k: 도로는 식물 종의 이동을 촉진해 토착 식물과 경쟁을 일으키고, 동물의 서식지를 분할해 먹이 부족과 개체 수 감소를 초래한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: roads harm ecosystems by fragmenting habitats and spreading plants. Professor's example: yellow starthistle seeds carried by car tires outcompeting native plants in California, and Kit foxes losing food access and declining.

speakingQ4.g: Franchising eases a new business start by supplying the parent company's training and ready-made business plan, plus customers who already trust the brand name.
speakingQ4.k: 프랜차이즈는 기존 유명 브랜드의 교육과 사업 계획, 그리고 이미 형성된 고객 신뢰 덕분에 새 사업자가 쉽게 출발할 수 있게 해준다.

speakingQ4.g: Frogs in dry regions survive by sealing their skin with a waxy layer to block water loss, or by storing water in a stretchable bladder for use during long droughts.
speakingQ4.k: 건조한 환경에 사는 개구리는 피부를 코팅해 수분 손실을 막거나 방광에 물을 저장하는 방식으로 살아남는다.

speakingQ4.g: Artifacts last long when surroundings are dry or oxygen-poor, since these conditions stop the bacteria that cause decay from growing.
speakingQ4.k: 유물이 오래 보존되는 것은 박테리아 번식을 억제하는 건조한 환경과 산소가 거의 없는 환경 덕분이다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4: concept of environmental conditions that inhibit decay bacteria; professor's examples are Egyptian desert tombs with preserved wall paintings (aridity) and a sunken Mediterranean ship with intact vases in oxygen-free mud (lack of oxygen).

speakingQ4.g: Snails survive hot, dry conditions by seeking shade and cooler surfaces, then sealing their shells and entering a dormant state to conserve moisture.
speakingQ4.k: 달팽이가 더위와 건조함을 피하기 위해 그늘로 이동하고, 여름에는 껍질 입구를 막아 수분을 지키며 휴면하는 방식

speakingQ4.g: The camera's invention changed painting in two ways: painters used photos as a realistic reference, and others moved toward abstraction to distinguish their work from photography.
speakingQ4.k: 사진기의 발명이 화가들에게 사실적 묘사의 도구가 되거나, 사진과 차별화하기 위해 비사실적·추상적 화풍을 택하게 만들었다는 설명
speakingQ4.c: Concept: photography reshaped painting both as a practical reference and as a push toward abstraction; Example: photos of a galloping horse's legs in midair helped painters depict motion, and abstract painters used unnatural skin colors like green, purple, or blue.

speakingQ4.g: As ancient economies grew more complex, people shifted from bartering to using money and began trading over long distances, as illustrated by Romans obtaining silk from China.
speakingQ4.k: 고대 문명이 발전하면서 화폐 사용과 먼 지역과의 교역이라는 경제 변화가 나타났으며, 이를 예시로 설명함
speakingQ4.c: Concept: money replaced barter and long-distance trade expanded; professor's example: a baker buying a coat with money, and Romans acquiring Chinese silk.

speakingQ4.g: Animals living at high altitudes develop strong muscles and specially shaped feet to climb steep slopes and keep their footing on ice and rock.
speakingQ4.k: 고산 동물들은 가파른 경사와 미끄러운 빙설을 이동하기 위해 강한 근육과 특수한 발 구조를 발달시켰다.
speakingQ4.c: concept-example: the professor explains that mountain animals need strength and sure footing to move on steep, slippery terrain, using mountain goats for muscles and bighorn sheep for feet.

speakingQ4.g: Salespeople can overcome customer hesitations either by highlighting a standout product feature that outweighs the concern or by demonstrating the product in action to show the worry is unfounded.
speakingQ4.k: 판매원이 고객의 우려를 해소하는 두 가지 전략: 제품의 특별한 장점으로 상쇄하기와 실제 시연으로 불안 덜어주기
speakingQ4.c: Concept: two sales strategies for answering customer objections (highlighting a standout feature; demonstrating the product). Professor's example: a salesperson selling a portable laptop who stresses its speed for a price worry and physically shows how easily it can be carried for a portability worry.

speakingQ4.g: Play helps children feel more in control amid dependence on adults and offers a safe outlet for impulses like destructiveness that would be unacceptable in real life.
speakingQ4.k: 아이들의 놀이는 통제감을 키우고 파괴적 충동을 안전하게 분출하게 해 정서 발달에 도움이 된다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: play as a source of psychological benefits; professor's example: a child building blocks and then knocking the tower down during play.

speakingQ4.g: A prolonged drought can drive animals to gather at the last remaining water source, and if that source dries up, the species can die out.
speakingQ4.k: 가뭄이 길어져 마지막 남은 물웅덩이가 마르면서 그곳에 모였던 동물들이 떼죽음을 당해 멸종에 이른 사례
speakingQ4.c: Concept: drought forces animals to crowd around the final water source, so when it dries up they perish; Professor's example: clusters of ancient giant bird bones found near a dried-up lake in Australia.

speakingQ4.g: Instead of just hunting for food, some animals actively tend and nurture their food sources over time.
speakingQ4.k: 일부 동물은 먹이를 찾아다니는 대신 먹이원을 직접 돌보고 키운다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: animals cultivating food sources; professor's examples: damselfish guarding seaweed from competing plants, and black ants protecting and raising aphids for their sweet liquid.

speakingQ4.g: Forest fires can help some animals by making prey easier for predators to catch and by turning hostile habitats into safe places for raising young.
speakingQ4.k: 산불은 일부 동물에게 사냥 기회와 번식 환경을 제공해 이득이 될 수 있다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: forest fires benefit certain animals by improving predators' food access and creating breeding sites. Example: wild turkeys catch insects fleeing the flames, and beetles lay eggs in fire-killed trees whose chemical defenses no longer work.

speakingQ4.g: Some fish generate electricity in their bodies, which helps them hunt prey and sense obstacles in their surroundings.
speakingQ4.k: 일부 물고기는 몸에서 전기를 만들어 먹이를 잡고 주변 장애물을 감지하는 데 활용한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: fish produce electric fields that aid survival; professor's examples: the electric eel stuns smaller fish to capture prey, and the knife fish detects nearby rocks by sensing disturbances in its electric field.

speakingQ4.g: Memories stick better when we already know the subject or when the thing stands out as unusual.
speakingQ4.k: 사람은 기존 지식이 있거나 특이한 것일수록 과거의 일을 더 잘 기억한다는 설명
speakingQ4.c: concept: memory strength depends on prior knowledge and distinctiveness; example: a classical music concert (knowledgeable vs. novice attendees) and a large class where unusual students are remembered

speakingQ4.g: Domesticating animals gave early humans a dependable meat supply and additional foods, with goats as the leading example.
speakingQ4.k: 동물 사육은 초기 인류에게 안정적인 고기 공급과 다양한 식품을 제공했으며, 염소가 그 대표적 예이다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: domestication made food supply reliable and more varied; professor's example: goats that could be herded, eaten for meat, and milked for products like yogurt and cheese.

speakingQ4.g: Advertising can harm the environment in two ways: it wastes resources by reaching people who have no use for the product, and it spoils natural scenery by blocking views.
speakingQ4.k: 광고는 필요 없는 소비자에게 자원을 낭비하게 하고, 자연 경관의 아름다움을 가로막아 환경에 부정적 영향을 준다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: advertising's two environmental costs (wasted resources, damaged scenery); Example: a rental tenant receiving a kitchen-renovation mailer, and roadside billboards ruining a mountain view.

speakingQ4.g: Living in groups brings two drawbacks for animals: a large gathering is easier for predators to spot, and in crowded groups parents can struggle to recognize and feed their own young.
speakingQ4.k: 동물이 무리 지어 사는 데는 포식자에게 쉽게 발견되는 위험과 새끼를 제대로 돌보지 못하는 문제라는 두 가지 단점이 있다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4: concept of group-living disadvantages; professor's examples are sardines hunted by whales (visibility to predators) and bats in a crowded cave feeding other mothers' babies (difficulty identifying own young).

speakingQ4.g: Animals use physical traits to survive predators, either by defensive structures that block attacks or offensive ones that deter them, illustrated with turtles and porcupines.
speakingQ4.k: 동물의 방어적·공격적 보호 적응 유형과 거북이·호저의 예시
speakingQ4.c: concept-example: defensive adaptations block predators (turtle's shell); offensive adaptations threaten them (porcupine's quills)

speakingQ4.g: Animals in groups rely on symbolic display behaviors, both threatening ones to avoid fights and friendly ones to reconcile afterward, to keep the group united.
speakingQ4.k: 동물들은 집단의 결속을 지키려고 위협 행동과 화해 행동 같은 과시적 신호를 사용한다
speakingQ4.c: Q4: concept of display behaviors (threatening and friendly) and the professor's baboon example (fruit dispute: stares and grunts, then fight followed by hugs and friendly noises)

speakingQ4.g: Appeals to people's sense of civic duty can get them to voluntarily reduce environmental harm, as shown by campaigns like Smokey the Bear and early community recycling.
speakingQ4.k: 환경 문제 해결에서 도덕적 의무감에 호소하는 자발적 설득 정책의 효과
speakingQ4.c: concept-example: the professor defines moral suasion as voluntary, duty-based persuasion and illustrates it with the Smokey the Bear campaign and early community recycling programs.

speakingQ4.g: Food spoils mainly because bacteria multiply in it, so controlling temperature and moisture to slow bacterial growth is the key way to preserve food.
speakingQ4.k: 음식이 상하는 것은 세균 번식 때문이며, 온도와 수분을 조절해 세균 성장을 늦추면 식품을 더 오래 보관할 수 있다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: lowering temperature and moisture slows bacterial growth and preserves food. Professor's examples: fish frozen versus left in the sun, and powdered milk versus liquid milk.

speakingQ4.g: Animals have an internal biological clock that runs slightly off 24 hours, and external light cues are needed to keep it synchronized.
speakingQ4.k: 동물은 체내 생체시계를 가지지만, 빛과 어둠 같은 외부 신호가 그 주기를 24시간에 맞춰 조정한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: an internal clock combined with external light cues sets the daily cycle. Professor's example: flying squirrels kept in constant darkness drifted to a shorter cycle, then realigned to a 24-hour schedule once exposed to daylight again.

speakingQ4.g: Infant attachment is driven more by comfort from warm physical contact than by feeding, as shown by a monkey study in which the infants preferred a soft surrogate mother even when the wire mother fed them.
speakingQ4.k: 아기와 양육자 사이의 애착은 젖을 먹이는 것보다 따뜻한 신체 접촉에 더 크게 좌우된다는 개념이며, 원숭이 실험이 이를 뒷받침한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: contact comfort, not feeding, forms the infant-caregiver bond; Example: baby monkeys raised with a cloth mother and a wire mother spent most of their time with the cloth mother regardless of which one fed them.

speakingQ4.g: Railroad expansion transformed American commerce by letting firms sell nationwide and build factories where raw materials had to be shipped in.
speakingQ4.k: 철도 확장이 상품의 전국 판매와 원자재 운송을 가능하게 해 미국 기업 활동을 바꿨다는 강의
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: railroads expanded markets and factory locations; professor's example: a clock company selling nationwide and southern factories powered by imported coal

speakingQ4.g: Stores attract buyers by bundling a free extra that appeals to shoppers, which both closes hesitant sales right away and brings customers back for later purchases.
speakingQ4.k: 매장이 주력 상품에 덧붙여 관심 있을 만한 무료 제공품을 끼워 팔아 즉각적인 판매와 고객 재방문을 동시에 늘리는 전략
speakingQ4.c: Q4 concept: 'second interest' (a free bonus tied to a main purchase); professor's examples: a free video game with a new computer for immediate sales, and free monthly computer lessons to retain customers who later buy accessories.

speakingQ4.g: When buying expensive items, consumers lower their sense of risk either by researching products thoroughly or by sticking with a brand they have trusted before.
speakingQ4.k: 고가 제품을 살 때 느끼는 위험을 줄이기 위해 소비자는 충분히 조사하거나 믿을 만한 브랜드에 계속 충성하는 방식을 쓴다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: consumers reduce perceived purchase risk through thorough research and brand loyalty; Example: a buyer reads expert reviews and asks owners before buying a computer, and a family returns to a car maker whose vehicle performed well.

speakingQ4.g: The professor compares two hypotheses for why dinosaurs died out: an asteroid-caused food shortage and volcanic-driven global warming that skewed reptile birth ratios.
speakingQ4.k: 공룡 멸종을 설명하는 두 가지 가설, 즉 소행성 충돌로 인한 식량 부족과 화산 활동으로 인한 기온 상승을 비교한다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: two competing theories of dinosaur extinction. Example: an asteroid's dust blocking sunlight starves plants and the food chain, and volcanic gases trap heat, shifting egg-temperature-dependent sex ratios toward males.

speakingQ4.g: Stores bundle products at a discount to push customers into buying more than planned and to clear out unsold older items.
speakingQ4.k: 상점이 여러 제품을 묶어 저렴하게 팔아 고객의 추가 구매를 유도하고 재고를 처리하는 방법을 설명한다.
speakingQ4.c: concept-example: the professor defines bundling, then illustrates it with a computer-and-printer example and a computer-plus-old-games example.

speakingQ4.g: Fast animals survive better because of physical adaptations such as tough foot pads and powerful, long legs, with the cheetah as the main example.
speakingQ4.k: 동물이 빠르게 달리는 능력은 사냥과 도피를 돕는 신체 적응에서 비롯되며, 치타가 대표적 예시다.
speakingQ4.c: concept-example: the professor explains that speed-linked physical traits (tough feet, strong long legs) help animals hunt and escape, illustrated by the cheetah's foot pads and leg structure.

speakingQ4.g: Animals blend into surroundings in two ways: a fixed match for those that stay in one environment, and an adjustable match for those that move between environments.
speakingQ4.k: 동물이 주변 환경의 색이나 모양을 닮아 몸을 숨기는 방식은, 평생 같은 환경에 머무는지 여러 환경을 이동하는지에 따라 고정형과 적응형으로 나뉜다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: protective resemblance is divided into permanent and adaptive types depending on whether the animal's environment stays the same; Example: a frog with a fixed brown, leaf-like look versus a lizard that changes color to match whatever ground or plants it is on.

speakingQ4.g: Decentralization gives local branch managers decision-making power, but it can make choices that benefit one location while hurting the whole company, and it can lead to inconsistent policies that frustrate customers.
speakingQ4.k: 여러 지점을 둔 대기업이 권한을 지점 관리자에게 넘기는 분권화는 지점 이익을 우선해 회사 전체에 해를 끼치고, 정책이 지역마다 달라 고객 불만을 낳을 수 있다.
speakingQ4.c: Concept: decentralization shifts decision-making from headquarters to local branches; professor's example: a clothing chain's struggling store where a local manager spends on advertising instead of closing it, and a store that refuses returns, upsetting customers.

speakingQ4.g: Fire is a natural and beneficial part of many ecosystems; controlled burns help pine forests regenerate and open space that attracts new plant and animal life.
speakingQ4.k: 산불은 생태계 유지에 필수적인 자연 과정이어서, 통제된 불이 숲의 재생과 야생동물 서식지 확보에 도움을 준다.
speakingQ4.c: Q4: concept of controlled fire as ecological tool; professor's example is pine trees whose cones open when resin melts from heat, releasing seeds, plus fire thinning dense forest to let in sunlight.

speakingQ4.s: predator hunting strategies in animal groups
speakingQ4.g: Predators overcome the defensive advantage of group living by singling out a conspicuous individual or by scattering the group to isolate one animal.
speakingQ4.k: 무리 지어 사는 동물을 포식자가 공략하는 두 가지 방법: 눈에 띄는 개체를 노리거나 무리를 흩어 놓기
speakingQ4.c: Concept: predators isolate one individual from a group by spotting a distinctive one or breaking the group apart. Professor's examples: a fish predator chasing the oddly colored member of a school, and a shark whipping its tail through a fish group to scatter it.

speakingQ4.g: Animals store food in different ways depending on their abilities: some guard one big pile, while weaker ones spread their supplies across many hidden spots and rely on memory.
speakingQ4.k: 동물들이 먹이를 저장하는 방식은 능력에 따라 달라지며, 한곳에 모아 지키는 전략과 여러 곳에 흩어 숨기는 전략이 있다.
